subject: Role of epsilon component in linear predictor

messages.author: e447af1cc53e57ee
messages.subject: Role of epsilon component in linear predictor
parts:
Hello,

I have a hierarchical model and am trying to draw replications of my dataset from the posterior predictive distribution. After some experimentation, I have managed to get myself rather confused about what I suspect is a simple matter. I hope that someone can easily set me straight. For the record, I'm aware that I can do an "NA replicate" trick to get posterior predictive draws as in this thread, but I'm sufficiently disturbed by my lack of clarity here that I have the basics right first, rather than just blindly applying recipes! :)

Based on the Intro PDF, I understand that the linear predictor eta_i is composed of my model terms as well as an iid epsilon_i  ~ N(0, lambda_eta). Then in addition to this, there is the "family noise", in my case student-T with unknown df and scale. I have an identity link.

If this is the case, then (based on the student-t likelihood documentation) I would expect that I should be able to do the following to draw from the posterior predictive. First obtain S posterior draws using inla.posterior.sample, and then for each draw s in 1, ..., S take the predicted values of eta_i from draw$latent -- call this vector eta_s -- and then one joint posterior predictive draw should be eta_s + rt(N, df=draw$hyperparam['df for t'])/sqrt(draw$hyperparam['precision for t'])

The problem is that, when I do this, the groups in the simulated replicates are all way more dispersed than they should be. This happens even with an intercept-only model, so it is not a matter of overfitting. It also happens if I use a plain Gaussian likelihood and eta_s + rnorm(N, sd=sqrt(1/draw$hyperparam['gaussian precision'])). Too much noise is being added.

Strangely, if I just take eta_s without adding the observation noise term, then I get summary statistics which behave roughly as I would expect. Which got me wondering about the epsilon_eta term -- is this actually where the likelihood comes in? It seems doubtful since the intro pretty clearly says without qualification that this is Gaussian and separate from the likelihood pi. However, it is strange to me that the model summary output says nothing about the estimated precision lambda_eta -- only the likelihood-related parameters. But of course everything seems strange when you don't understand it ;)

Would someone be so kind as to put me back on the right path? What is the role of these epsilon_i, and how are they distinct from the observation noise under identity link and Gaussian/t likelihood? Maybe in this special "degenerate" case, I need to use a hack like in the linked thread (setting the family to a fixed, high precision) to prevent overspecification? But then I'm limited to Gaussian (and not T)?

Many thanks,
Jonathan

messages.author: 9940b4fcc153c7d7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Role of epsilon component in linear predictor
parts:
Do I understand you correct in that your
y = epsilon1 + epsilon 2 + more
Where epsilon1 is the likelihood (gaussian or student t), and epsilon2 is in the linear predictor?

This model does not really make sense, as you cannot separate the two independent noise contributions. I would expect this to lead to inflated variances. The model does not know which component to use, and so, in fitting it is using either, and in  prediction, it is using them both.

I do not think INLA works on this model, but as the model does not make sense, it is not considered a problem.
(If you fix the hyper-parameters in epsilon2, INLA should be able to fit the model. But this does not make the model sensible.)


Does that help?
Haakon

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Role of epsilon component in linear predictor
parts:
That "two epsilons model" is not the model I want to have, but I fear it may be the model I *do* have ;) What I want is a for the i-th observation for subject s to be:

y_si = alpha + X_s*Beta + gamma_s + f_s(time) + epsilon_si

with:
- common intercept alpha
- linear regression coefficients Beta
- iid, subject-level random intercepts gamma_s
- a subject-specific, smooth random walk component f_s
- Student's t-distributed observation noise epsilon_si, with unknown scale and df

I then call INLA like this:

inla( y~1+X1+X2+...+f(subjectID, model="iid")+f(time,model="rw1",replicate=subject), family="T", control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, link=1))

Am I totally off track with this?

-Jonathan
